s:
With reference to the original Article 31C inserted by the Twenty-fifth Amendment, consider the following statements:
1. Laws giving effect to Articles 39(b) and 39(c) were protected from challenge under Articles 14 and 19.
2. The protection also extended to Article 31.
3. A declaration by the law-making authority that the law gave effect to the relevant policy could not be questioned in court.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: The original Article 31C contained both protections: specified laws were protected from Articles 14, 19 and 31 challenges, and the declaration that they implemented the policy was placed beyond judicial questioning.
tq: Separate the two limbs of Article 31C and check the additional protection against Article 31.
sec: Article 31C - inserted, extended, struck down  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following correctly describes the decision in Kesavananda Bharati relating to Article 31C?
o: The first provision was upheld and the second provision was struck down.
The first provision was struck down and the second provision was upheld.
Both provisions of Article 31C were struck down.
Both provisions were upheld without limitation.
x: Kesavananda Bharati upheld the first part of Article 31C but struck down the second part, which excluded judicial review.
tq: Distinguish the first and second provisions rather than treating Article 31C as a single indivisible rule.
sec: Article 31C - inserted, extended, struck down  [APPSC]

s: The Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976 extended the protection of Article 31C to laws implementing:
o: Only Articles 39(b) and 39(c)
Only Fundamental Duties
Any Directive Principle of State Policy
Only Article 14
x: The Forty-second Amendment extended Article 31C from laws implementing Articles 39(b) and 39(c) to laws implementing any DPSP.
tq: Use the scope comparison between the original and amended versions of Article 31C.
sec: Article 31C - inserted, extended, struck down  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following was the effect of the judgment in Minerva Mills on Article 31C?
o: The extension of Article 31C to all DPSPs was struck down, restoring its application to Articles 39(b) and 39(c).
The entire Article 31C was repealed.
Article 31C was extended to Fundamental Duties.
The bar on judicial review in the original Article 31C was restored.
x: Minerva Mills struck down the Forty-second Amendment's extension of Article 31C to all DPSPs. Its protection consequently remained confined to laws implementing Articles 39(b) and 39(c).
tq: Track what was struck down and what remained after the later judgment.
sec: Article 31C - inserted, extended, struck down  [APPSC]

s: The continued operation of the original Article 31C, as upheld in Kesavananda Bharati, was reaffirmed in which of the following decisions in 2024?
o: R.C. Cooper
Sanjeev Coke
Property Owners Association
Madhav Rao Scindia
x: The Property Owners Association decision of 2024 affirmed that the original Article 31C, as upheld in Kesavananda Bharati, continues in force.
tq: Match the recent decision with the specific constitutional proposition it reaffirmed.
sec: Article 31C - inserted, extended, struck down  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following cases is associated with the proposition that Fundamental Rights prevail over Directive Principles in the event of conflict?
o: State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan
In re Kerala Education Bill
Minerva Mills v. Union of India
Sanjeev Coke v. Bharat Coking Coal
x: In State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951), the Supreme Court held that DPSPs were subsidiary to Fundamental Rights when the two conflicted.
tq: Identify the landmark case directly associated with the stated constitutional conflict.
sec: Case → position on FR-DPSP relationship; chronology  [other exams]

s: The judgment in State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan primarily involved the striking down of a Madras order relating to:
o: Abolition of privy purses
Nationalisation of coking coal
Communal allocation of seats in educational admissions
Compensation for acquired estates
x: The communal order regulating admissions was struck down as violating Article 29(2). The decision subsequently led to the insertion of Article 15(4).
tq: Link the case to the concrete administrative order that triggered the constitutional ruling.
sec: Case → position on FR-DPSP relationship; chronology  [other exams]

s: The immediate constitutional consequence of the Champakam Dorairajan judgment was the insertion of:
o: Article 368(3)
Article 13(4)
Article 31C
Article 15(4)
x: The First Constitutional Amendment inserted Article 15(4) after the Champakam Dorairajan judgment.
tq: Use the case-to-amendment linkage rather than confusing it with later Golaknath-related amendments.
sec: Amendments responding to courts  [other exams]

s: In re Kerala Education Bill, 1958 is associated with which of the following approaches?
o: Harmonious construction, giving effect to both Fundamental Rights and DPSPs as far as possible
Abolition of judicial review
Parliament's inability to amend any Fundamental Right
Complete supremacy of DPSPs over Fundamental Rights
x: In re Kerala Education Bill adopted harmonious construction, requiring both Parts III and IV to be given effect as far as possible, while Fundamental Rights continued to prevail in case of direct conflict.
tq: Distinguish harmonious construction from either absolute rights supremacy or DPSP supremacy.
sec: Case → position on FR-DPSP relationship; chronology  [other exams]

s: Which one of the following correctly states the ratio of Golaknath v. State of Punjab?
o: Parliament could amend Fundamental Rights without limitation.
Only Article 39(b) could be amended by Parliament.
Parliament could not amend Fundamental Rights; they were given a transcendental position.
Fundamental Rights and DPSPs had equal absolute primacy.
x: Golaknath held that Parliament could not amend Fundamental Rights and described them as having a transcendental position. The Court also applied prospective overruling.
tq: Test the distinctive holding of Golaknath against the later Kesavananda position.
sec: Case → position on FR-DPSP relationship; chronology  [other exams]

s: The doctrine of prospective overruling was applied in which of the following cases?
o: Golaknath
Champakam Dorairajan
Minerva Mills
A.K. Gopalan
x: The Supreme Court applied prospective overruling in Golaknath v. State of Punjab.
tq: Associate the procedural effect of the judgment with the correct case.
sec: Case → position on FR-DPSP relationship; chronology  [other exams]

s:
With reference to Kesavananda Bharati, consider the following statements:
1. Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights.
2. Parliament cannot alter the basic structure of the Constitution.
3. The judgment upheld the second provision of Article 31C excluding judicial review.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: Kesavananda Bharati held that Parliament could amend Fundamental Rights but could not destroy the basic structure. It struck down, rather than upheld, the second provision of Article 31C.
tq: Combine the basic-structure holding with the specific Article 31C ruling and identify the reversed statement.
sec: Case → position on FR-DPSP relationship; chronology  [other exams]

s: The central constitutional principle laid down in Minerva Mills was that:
o: DPSPs have absolute primacy over Fundamental Rights.
Fundamental Rights have absolute primacy over DPSPs in every circumstance.
Harmony and balance between Parts III and IV form part of the basic structure.
Parliament has unlimited power to amend the Constitution.
x: Minerva Mills held that harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights in Part III and DPSPs in Part IV are part of the basic structure; absolute primacy to either would destroy that balance.
tq: Choose the balanced constitutional principle over extreme claims of absolute supremacy.
sec: Case → position on FR-DPSP relationship; chronology  [other exams]

s: Which one of the following statements regarding Sanjeev Coke v. Bharat Coking Coal is correct?
o: It held that Parliament could never amend Fundamental Rights.
It struck down the nationalisation of coking coal under Article 39(b).
It invalidated the original Article 31C.
It upheld coking coal nationalisation under Article 39(b) and read material resources as including privately owned resources.
x: Sanjeev Coke upheld the coking coal nationalisation law under Article 39(b) and interpreted material resources as including privately owned resources. It also doubted the Minerva Mills Article 31C ruling in obiter.
tq: Match the case with its sector-specific ruling and its interpretation of material resources.
sec: Case → position on FR-DPSP relationship; chronology  [other exams]

s:
Arrange the following cases in chronological order:
A. Minerva Mills
B. A.K. Gopalan
C. Sanjeev Coke
D. Golaknath
E. State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan
F. Kesavananda Bharati
o: B, E, D, F, A, C
E, B, D, F, C, A
B, D, E, F, A, C
B, E, F, D, A, C
x: The correct sequence is A.K. Gopalan (1950), Champakam Dorairajan (1951), Golaknath (1967), Kesavananda Bharati (1973), Minerva Mills (1980), and Sanjeev Coke (1983).
tq: Fix the earliest and latest cases first, then place the intervening judgments by year.
sec: Case → position on FR-DPSP relationship; chronology  [other exams]

s: Which one of the following correctly describes the decision in A.K. Gopalan (1950)?
o: It established harmony between Parts III and IV as basic structure.
It adopted a narrow reading of Fundamental Rights and examined only procedure.
It upheld nationalisation under Article 39(b).
It held that Fundamental Rights could never be amended.
x: A.K. Gopalan adopted a narrow reading of Fundamental Rights, with the Court examining only the prescribed procedure.
tq: Identify the earliest case's limited procedural approach before considering later doctrines.
sec: Case → position on FR-DPSP relationship; chronology  [other exams]

s: Which amendment inserted Articles 15(4), 31A and 31B and created the Ninth Schedule?
o: The First Constitutional Amendment, 1951
The Fourth Constitutional Amendment, 1955
The Seventeenth Constitutional Amendment, 1964
The Twenty-fourth Constitutional Amendment, 1971
x: The First Amendment Act, 1951, followed Champakam and land-reform cases and inserted Article 15(4), Articles 31A and 31B, and the Ninth Schedule.
tq: Use the cluster of constitutional changes to identify the amendment rather than one isolated provision.
sec: Amendments responding to courts  [other exams]

s: The Fourth Constitutional Amendment Act, 1955 made which aspect non-justiciable?
o: The classification of privately owned material resources
The adequacy of compensation
The President's assent to constitutional amendments
The existence of Fundamental Duties
x: The Fourth Amendment made the adequacy of compensation non-justiciable.
tq: Distinguish the subject of compensation adequacy from later changes replacing compensation with amount.
sec: Amendments responding to courts  [other exams]

s:
Consider the following statements about the Seventeenth Constitutional Amendment Act, 1964:
1. It widened the meaning of ‘estate’ under Article 31A.
2. It provided that land under personal cultivation could be acquired only at market value.
3. It inserted Article 31C.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: The Seventeenth Amendment widened ‘estate’ in Article 31A and dealt with land under personal cultivation. Article 31C was inserted later by the Twenty-fifth Amendment.
tq: Separate the land-reform changes of the Seventeenth Amendment from the later Article 31C amendment.
sec: Amendments responding to courts  [other exams]

s: The Twenty-fourth Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971 was enacted in response to Golaknath and provided that:
o: Privy purses would be abolished.
The adequacy of compensation could be examined by courts.
Parliament could amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights.
Only DPSPs could be amended by Parliament.
x: The Twenty-fourth Amendment responded to Golaknath by affirming Parliament's power to amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights. It added Article 13(4) and Article 368(3), and made presidential assent mandatory.
tq: Link the amendment to the judgment it was intended to overcome and identify its broad power.
sec: Amendments responding to courts  [other exams]

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Twenty-fifth Amendment — inserted Article 31C and replaced ‘compensation’ by ‘amount’
Twenty-fourth Amendment — abolished privy purses
Twenty-sixth Amendment — extended Article 31C to all DPSPs
Forty-second Amendment — inserted Article 15(4)
x: The Twenty-fifth Amendment replaced ‘compensation’ by ‘amount’ and inserted Article 31C. The Twenty-fourth Amendment dealt with Parliament's amending power, the Twenty-sixth abolished privy purses, and the Forty-second extended Article 31C to all DPSPs.
tq: Start from the sure amendment-provision pair and reject swapped amendment responses.
sec: Amendments responding to courts  [other exams]

s: The Twenty-fifth Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971 was associated, among other things, with which of the following changes?
o: Widening of ‘estate’ under Article 31A
Abolition of privy purses
Replacement of the term ‘compensation’ by ‘amount’
Insertion of Article 15(4)
x: The Twenty-fifth Amendment replaced ‘compensation’ by ‘amount’ and inserted Article 31C. Article 15(4), the widening of ‘estate’, and abolition of privy purses belonged to other amendments.
tq: Discriminate among closely timed amendments by their precise key changes.
sec: Amendments responding to courts  [other exams]

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched in relation to the Twenty-sixth Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971?
o: Champakam case — extension of Article 31C to all DPSPs
Golaknath case — insertion of Article 15(4)
Privy Purses case — abolition of privy purses and privileges of former rulers
Bank Nationalisation case — creation of the Ninth Schedule
x: The Twenty-sixth Amendment responded to the Privy Purses case associated with Madhav Rao Scindia and abolished privy purses and the privileges of former rulers.
tq: Match the case, amendment and constitutional consequence without swapping neighbouring historical responses.
sec: Amendments responding to courts  [other exams]

s: The Forty-second Constitutional Amendment's extension of Article 31C to all Directive Principles was later invalidated because it was held to:
o: Abolish the Ninth Schedule
Destroy the harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights and DPSPs
Create Article 15(4) without parliamentary approval
Make compensation justiciable
x: Minerva Mills struck down the extension because giving unlimited primacy to all DPSPs destroyed the constitutionally required harmony and balance between Parts III and IV.
tq: Apply the basic-structure principle to the consequence of granting one constitutional part absolute primacy.
sec: Amendments responding to courts  [other exams]

s: Which one of the following correctly describes the justiciability of Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy?
o: Fundamental Rights are non-enforceable, whereas Directive Principles are enforceable
Fundamental Rights are enforceable, whereas Directive Principles are non-enforceable
Both are enforceable by courts in the same manner
Neither Fundamental Rights nor Directive Principles is recognised by courts
x: Fundamental Rights are justiciable and can be enforced through courts. Directive Principles are non-justiciable under Article 37, though they are fundamental in the governance of the country.
tq: Test the central FR–DPSP distinction by separating enforceability from constitutional importance.
sec: FR vs DPSP - differences

s: The Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles respectively derive their conceptual sources from which of the following countries?
o: United Kingdom and Canada
United States of America and Ireland
Canada and Australia
Ireland and United States of America
x: The source of Fundamental Rights is the Constitution of the United States of America, whereas the Directive Principles were inspired by the Constitution of Ireland.
tq: Use the source-country pair as a direct constitutional comparison.
sec: FR vs DPSP - differences

s: Which of the following best expresses the difference in the general nature of Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles?
o: Fundamental Rights are mainly positive commands, while Directive Principles mainly restrain the State
Directive Principles impose criminal liability, while Fundamental Rights impose civil liability
Fundamental Rights mainly restrain the State, while Directive Principles direct the State towards positive action
Both Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are mainly negative restrictions on the State
x: Fundamental Rights are mostly negative in character because they restrain State action. Directive Principles are positive directions intended to guide the State in promoting welfare.
tq: Discriminate between negative restraints and positive directions rather than between enforceability alone.
sec: FR vs DPSP - differences

s: Fundamental Rights primarily aim at political democracy and individual welfare, whereas Directive Principles primarily aim at
o: administrative centralisation and official privilege
judicial supremacy and territorial expansion
electoral competition and political party regulation
social and economic democracy and community welfare
x: Fundamental Rights emphasise political democracy and individual welfare. Directive Principles seek social and economic democracy along with community welfare.
tq: Match each constitutional part with its stated democratic and welfare objective.
sec: FR vs DPSP - differences

s: A law violating a Fundamental Right and a law violating a Directive Principle have which respective legal consequences?
o: The former may be void under Article 13, while the latter cannot be struck down merely for violating a Directive Principle
The former cannot be examined by courts, while the latter is void under Article 37
Both laws are automatically void under Article 13
Both laws are immune from judicial review
x: Article 13 makes laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights void to the extent of inconsistency. Courts cannot strike down a law solely because it violates a Directive Principle.
tq: Apply the constitutional consequence separately to an enforceable right and a non-justiciable directive.
sec: FR vs DPSP - differences

s: With reference to the constitutional status of Directive Principles, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: They are legally superior to all Fundamental Rights in every circumstance
They are enforceable only during a national emergency
They have no constitutional significance because Article 37 excludes them from governance
They are not enforceable in courts but are fundamental in the governance of the country
x: Directive Principles are non-justiciable, but Article 37 declares them fundamental in the governance of the country and makes it the duty of the State to apply them in making laws.
tq: Avoid the trap of equating non-enforceability with lack of constitutional importance.
sec: FR vs DPSP - differences

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Forty-Second Amendment attempted to extend Article 31C protection to laws implementing all Directive Principles.
2. The Forty-Fourth Amendment gave all Directive Principles precedence over Articles 14 and 19.
3. The attempt to give all Directive Principles such precedence was struck down by the Supreme Court.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. The Forty-Second Amendment, not the Forty-Fourth, attempted to extend Article 31C to all Directive Principles, and that extension was struck down.
tq: Catch the amendment-year swap by identifying which amendment made the attempt and which did not.
sec: Article 39(b) and (c) laws - protection from Articles 14 and 19

s:
The Forty-Second Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 was associated with which of the following measures?
1. Extending Article 31C protection to laws implementing all Directive Principles
2. Claiming unlimited amending power under Article 368
3. Giving precedence to all Directive Principles over Articles 14 and 19
Which of the above is/are correct?
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: The Forty-Second Amendment attempted all three measures. The extension of Article 31C and the claim of unlimited amending power were subsequently invalidated in the relevant constitutional litigation.
tq: Recognise a cluster of provisions associated with one amendment instead of isolating only its best-known feature.
sec: Article 39(b) and (c) laws - protection from Articles 14 and 19

s: Which of the following was held in Minerva Mills v. Union of India?
o: Parliament possesses unlimited power to amend the Constitution
All Directive Principles automatically override Articles 14, 19 and 21
The balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is a basic feature, and Parliament's limited amending power is itself basic
Article 31C was completely removed from the Constitution
x: Minerva Mills held that limited amending power is a basic feature and that harmony between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is essential. The expansion of Article 31C to all Directive Principles was struck down, while its application to Article 39(b) and (c) survived.
tq: Use the basic-structure trap: an amendment cannot destroy the Constitution's own limited amending power.
sec: Article 39(b) and (c) laws - protection from Articles 14 and 19

s: Which one of the following additional propositions was recognised in Minerva Mills in relation to an Emergency proclamation?
o: It is subject only to review by the Election Commission
It can be reviewed only by a joint sitting of Parliament
It is permanently beyond judicial review
It is subject to judicial review
x: Minerva Mills recognised that an Emergency proclamation is not wholly immune from judicial review.
tq: Identify the constitutional authority involved in reviewing an executive emergency action.
sec: Article 39(b) and (c) laws - protection from Articles 14 and 19

s: After the decision in Minerva Mills, the relationship between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is best described as one in which
o: Directive Principles permanently prevail over Fundamental Rights in every matter
Fundamental Rights permanently prevail over Directive Principles in every matter
both are complementary and form an integrated constitutional scheme
both are independent and cannot be read together
x: Minerva Mills rejected the idea of an absolute conflict and treated Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles as complementary components of an integrated constitutional scheme.
tq: Use the harmonious-construction approach instead of assuming an absolute hierarchy.
sec: Harmonious construction; Part III-Part IV balance as basic structure

s: The statement “Fundamental Rights are the means and Directive Principles are the ends” signifies that
o: Fundamental Rights provide the framework through which the social and economic objectives of Directive Principles may be pursued
Directive Principles have no relationship with Fundamental Rights
Fundamental Rights may be suspended whenever a Directive Principle is invoked
Directive Principles are enforceable through the same remedies as Fundamental Rights
x: Fundamental Rights provide rights-based means, while Directive Principles express broader social and economic goals. The two are therefore to be understood together, not as competing constitutional compartments.
tq: Translate a constitutional maxim into its practical relationship between rights and goals.
sec: Harmonious construction; Part III-Part IV balance as basic structure

s:
Which of the following illustrates the use of a Directive Principle as an interpretive aid to expand the content of a Fundamental Right?
1. Article 45 read with Article 21 contributed to the recognition of the Right to Education under Article 21A.
2. Article 48A read with Article 21 supports the right to a healthy environment.
3. Directive Principles are entirely excluded from constitutional interpretation because they are non-justiciable.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Courts have used Directive Principles to interpret and enrich Fundamental Rights; non-justiciability does not exclude them from constitutional interpretation.
tq: Distinguish non-enforceability from non-relevance in constitutional interpretation.
sec: Harmonious construction; Part III-Part IV balance as basic structure

s: In testing the validity of a law based on a Directive Principle but alleged to abridge Fundamental Rights, the relevant constitutional standard includes
o: the non-justiciability of Directive Principles alone
only Article 37, without reference to Fundamental Rights
only Article 32 and the Ninth Schedule
the basic structure doctrine and the golden triangle of Articles 14, 19 and 21
x: The validity of such a law is examined against the basic structure doctrine and, in particular, the constitutional guarantees represented by Articles 14, 19 and 21, known as the golden triangle.
tq: Apply the controlling constitutional test rather than treating a DPSP objective as conclusive.
sec: Harmonious construction; Part III-Part IV balance as basic structure

s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Kesavananda Bharati — Amendments, including Ninth Schedule inclusions, cannot destroy the basic structure
2. Waman Rao — Post-24 April 1973 Ninth Schedule entries can be tested against the basic structure
3. I.R. Coelho — Every Ninth Schedule entry enjoys blanket immunity from judicial review
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: Pairs 1 and 2 are correctly matched. I.R. Coelho rejected blanket immunity and held that post-1973 entries may be invalid if they damage the basic structure or the essence of Articles 14, 19 and 21.
tq: Find the reversed proposition in a case-law match, especially where a judgment rejected an absolute rule.
sec: Harmonious construction; Part III-Part IV balance as basic structure

s:
Arrange the following decisions in chronological order:
A. I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu
B. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
C. Waman Rao v. Union of India
D. Minerva Mills v. Union of India
o: B, D, C, A
B, C, D, A
C, B, D, A
D, B, C, A
x: The correct sequence is Kesavananda Bharati (1973), Waman Rao (1981), Minerva Mills (1980), I.R. Coelho (2007) only if arranged by the dates stated? Actually Minerva Mills was decided in 1980 and therefore precedes Waman Rao. The correct chronological order is Kesavananda Bharati (1973), Minerva Mills (1980), Waman Rao (1981), I.R. Coelho (2007).
tq: Fix the dates first and then order the cases, paying particular attention to the close 1980–1981 sequence.
sec: Harmonious construction; Part III-Part IV balance as basic structure

s: Which one of the following statements regarding the Ninth Schedule is NOT correct?
o: Article 31B was inserted by the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951
The Ninth Schedule has remained confined to land reform laws and never expanded beyond them
The number of entries in it grew to more than 280
The Ninth Schedule was initially associated with protection for land reform laws from Fundamental Rights challenges
x: Statement c is not correct. Although the Ninth Schedule was initially intended for land reforms, its entries later grew to more than 280 and were not confined to that subject.
tq: Reject the absolute claim that an initially limited constitutional device never expanded.
sec: Harmonious construction; Part III-Part IV balance as basic structure

s: What was the significance of the cut-off date of 24 April 1973 laid down in Waman Rao?
o: Only laws enacted after the Forty-Fourth Amendment could be reviewed
All laws included in the Ninth Schedule before that date were automatically void
The date marked the commencement of Article 31C
Ninth Schedule entries made after that date could be tested against the basic structure
x: Waman Rao treated 24 April 1973 as the cut-off date and held that Ninth Schedule laws or entries added after it could be examined against the basic structure.
tq: Use the date as a legal cut-off rather than confusing it with the date of an amendment or provision.
sec: Harmonious construction; Part III-Part IV balance as basic structure

s: The decision in I.R. Coelho is significant because it held that
o: Ninth Schedule laws are completely beyond judicial review
only laws relating to land reforms can be placed in the Ninth Schedule
post-1973 Ninth Schedule entries may be invalid if they damage the basic structure or the essence of Articles 14, 19 and 21
Article 31B was repealed in its entirety
x: I.R. Coelho rejected blanket immunity. Post-1973 Ninth Schedule entries remain open to review if they damage the basic structure or the essential guarantees of Articles 14, 19 and 21.
tq: Identify the exception to immunity by connecting Ninth Schedule review with the golden triangle.
sec: Harmonious construction; Part III-Part IV balance as basic structure

s: Justice Chandrachud described Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles together as constituting the
o: code of administrative procedure
exclusive domain of the executive
conscience of the Constitution
framework of parliamentary privilege
x: Justice Chandrachud described Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles together as making up the conscience of the Constitution.
tq: Recall the distinctive judicial phrase attached to the combined constitutional role of Parts III and IV.
sec: Harmonious construction; Part III-Part IV balance as basic structure

s: Which of the following correctly states the latest Supreme Court position on the expression “material resources of the community” in Article 39(b)?
o: No privately owned resource can ever be a material resource of the community
Only resources owned by the Union Government can be covered
Whether a privately owned resource is covered depends on factors such as its nature, scarcity, effect on community well-being and the consequences of concentration in private hands
Every privately owned resource is automatically a material resource of the community
x: In Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra, the Supreme Court held that private ownership alone does not automatically bring a resource within Article 39(b). The determination depends on the resource and its effects on the community and concentration of wealth.
tq: Apply the latest multi-factor judicial test instead of choosing an absolute public-versus-private rule.
sec: Material resources of the community - latest SC view

s: Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra, decided on 5 November 2024, was decided by
o: a nine-judge Bench unanimously
a seven-judge Bench unanimously
a five-judge Bench by a 3:2 majority
a nine-judge Bench by a 7:2 majority
x: The case was decided on 5 November 2024 by a nine-judge Bench, with the relevant conclusion being reached by a 7:2 majority.
tq: Separate Bench strength from the majority ratio when handling a recent constitutional judgment.
sec: Material resources of the community - latest SC view

s: In Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra, the majority view was delivered by
o: Justice Y.V. Chandrachud as a dissenting judge
Chief Justice P.N. Bhagwati
Justice Krishna Iyer
Chief Justice D.Y. Chandrachud
x: The majority opinion in the November 2024 nine-judge Bench decision was delivered by Chief Justice D.Y. Chandrachud.
tq: Avoid the judge-name trap by distinguishing the current majority opinion from the earlier Krishna Iyer view.
sec: Material resources of the community - latest SC view

s:
Consider the following statements regarding the judicial history of Article 39(b):
1. In State of Karnataka v. Ranganatha Reddy (1977), Justice Krishna Iyer's minority view included privately owned resources within “material resources of the community”.
2. The broad view was followed in Sanjeev Coke (1983).
3. Property Owners Association rejected the proposition that every privately owned resource automatically falls within Article 39(b).
Which of the statements given above are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
x: All three statements are correct. The broad interpretation associated with Justice Krishna Iyer in Ranganatha Reddy was followed in Sanjeev Coke, while the 2024 Property Owners Association decision rejected its automatic application to every privately owned resource.
tq: Track the evolution of a legal proposition from an earlier minority view to its later qualification.
sec: Material resources of the community - latest SC view

s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Sanjeev Coke — 1983
Property Owners Association — 2024
Waman Rao — 2007
Ranganatha Reddy — 1977
x: Waman Rao was decided in 1981, not 2007. I.R. Coelho was the 2007 decision concerning the absence of blanket immunity for Ninth Schedule entries.
tq: Use the year mismatch to distinguish closely related constitutional cases.
sec: Material resources of the community - latest SC view

s: Which one of the following Articles was inserted by the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951, in response to the constitutional issue highlighted by the Champakam Dorairajan case?
o: Article 39(b)
Article 15(4)
Article 51A
Article 31C
x: Article 15(4) was inserted by the First Amendment Act, 1951, to enable special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes and for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

s: The First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951, altered the constitutional position concerning which of the following rights in the context of the Champakam Dorairajan controversy?
o: Right to constitutional remedies under Article 32
Right against exploitation under Article 23
Right to equality and non-discrimination under Article 15
Right to freedom of religion under Article 25
x: The amendment concerned Article 15, which deals with equality and non-discrimination, by inserting Article 15(4). This provision enabled special measures for specified backward classes, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

s: Which of the following best expresses the significance of the Minerva Mills judgment in the context of Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles?
o: It treated Directive Principles as legally irrelevant to constitutional interpretation.
It treated the balance between the two as part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution.
It confined constitutional amendments to matters relating to the Ninth Schedule.
It made every Directive Principle superior to every Fundamental Right without exception.
x: Minerva Mills made the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles part of the Basic Structure. It did not establish absolute supremacy for either category or limit amendments only to the Ninth Schedule.
tq: Apply the Basic Structure principle to distinguish constitutional balance from absolute supremacy.
